newsitem.title: USA: NYC council sees new agency selling debt in FY 98.
newsitem.headline: NYC council sees new agency selling debt in FY 98.

text.p: The New York City Council on Tuesday said it unanimously approved a plan creating a new borrowing arm, and looked for it to begin selling bonds for capital programs early in the 1998 fiscal year.

Albany lawmakers are expected to approve the measure on Wednesday, which is why the Council held its vote one day earlier. "Any time there's a window open in Albany, you jump through it," said Tom McMahon, director of finance, for the City Council.

Talks between Albany and New York City over the new financing arm, the New York City Transitional Finance Authority, broke down in late December, when the state Senate and Assembly held a special session. Gov George Pataki should get by March 1 the bill the Senate and Assembly now are expected to approve, a City Council spokeswoman said.

The City Council's finance director seemed a bit more confident than state and city comptrollers about Albany's willingness to extend the city's 12.5 percent personal income tax surcharge, which expired at year-end.
"It's clearly a concern, but ultimately we're confident that the city will hear us," said McMahon.
According to the Council, the new borrowing Authority would issue bonds over four years that would be backed by the city's personal income tax.

The Authority could only sell debt until the state constitution is amended to change the city's debt ceiling, a measure that could not be put to a vote before November, 1999. The new agency, which could sell up to $7.5 billion of bonds, would allow the city to keep paying for capital programs after it hits the debt cap--probably a month or so before its 1997 fiscal year ends on June 30.
The bill calls for the city's budget director to submit an annual statement of "debt affordability" when the executive budget is disclosed.
The Office of Management and Budget would be required to hold hearings on the statement, which would list the projects that would be funded, along with other information about the city's debt.
